records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name: RHS's dedicated Rosa banksiae page leads with the subtitle Banksia rose and lists Banksian rose and Lady Banks' rose as other common names, while NC State's page-title parenthetical lists Lady Banks, Lady Banks Rose (alphabetized list) and its Description opens with Lady Banks rose. Lady Banks Rose is used. The yellow 'Lutea' cultivar is kept separate: NC State says it differs only in its yellow flowers.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS (Potentially harmful field): 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' RHS Pets line: 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. The Pets line names no animal, and RHS gives no severity rating or symptom list. NC State's page for this species has no Poison block and no Problem for Cats/Dogs tags. The sources address different parts: NC State's Leaf Value To Gardener field reads Edible, with no preparation or amount, and its Fruit Value To Gardener field reads Good Cut; RHS says the fruit is not to be eaten.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: RHS's Pets line says the fruit is 'ornamental - not to be eaten' and names no animal (no cat or dog), and NC State's page for this species carries no Poison block and no Problem for Cats/Dogs tag. No admissible source scopes toxicity to cats or dogs.

is_edible left null: NC State's Leaf Value To Gardener field reads Edible with no preparation or amount, and its Fruit Value To Gardener reads Good Cut; RHS says the fruit is ornamental and not to be eaten and advises gloves when handling. The two statements concern different parts, and no source says the plant is grown or used for food. Generic rose-hip edibility is not carried over to this species.

Common-name split: RHS's dedicated page leads with Banksia rose (Other common names: Banksian rose, Lady Banks' rose). NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list reads Lady Banks, then Lady Banks Rose, and its Description opens 'Lady Banks rose is a big, sprawling, rambling shrub in the rose family (Rosaceae)'. The record lands under Lady Banks Rose, NC State's Description prose opener.

MoBot: reachable search results only showed pages for Rosa banksiae var. banksiae and the cultivar 'Lutea', both excluded as non-exact pages, and the plantfinder host could not be fetched. Clemson HGIC's Lady Banks page returned HTTP 403. Neither was used; the record rests on NC State and RHS only.

Lutea (yellow, double-flowered cultivar) is kept out of the species record; NC State says it differs only in its yellow flowers. NC State's cultivar list also names Alba Plena, Alboplena, Lutescens and var. normalis; none of their traits are used here.

Size: NC State gives Height 15-40 ft and Width 6-10 ft (used). RHS gives Max Height 4-8 metres (157-315 in) and Max Spread 2.5-4 metres (98-157 in), a narrower height range and wider spread. The differences are left unreconciled.
Bloom habit: NC State says the species blooms in early spring for about a month (Description: midspring to early summer) and has no prickles. No repeat-blooming care is implied.

water_regime left null: NC State's 'moist, but well-draining' is a soil description, and no admissible page gives a watering statement for this species. RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained', a soil-moisture descriptor rather than a watering cadence.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State says only 'acidic to neutral' with no numbers; RHS pH lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no ceiling or floor can be set.
fertilize fields left null: RHS's rose fertiliser advice sits in a Rosa-wide Cultivation paragraph not shown to be species-specific, and gives named seasons, not a number of days or a dilution.
chill_damage_f left null: RHS says only 'Liable to frost damage grown elsewhere' and rates it H5 with no onset temperature; NC State lists USDA zones 6a-10b (a survival range, not a damage onset).

is_houseplant is false: both sources treat it as an in-ground landscape climber/shrub (NC State Landscape Location Coastal, Pool/Hardscape, Rock Wall and Vertical Spaces; USDA zones 6a-10b) and no source addresses indoor culture. Humidity, light_fc, temperature, water interval and direct_sun_hours_max have no species-specific admissible figure.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' and its prose says 'It grows in full sun or partial shade', but its tag list reads '#partial shade tolerant', and RHS's structured Position field lists Full sun only, so part_shade was dropped.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. RHS's dedicated page renders "saw-toothed hydrangea" as its subtitle and lists "mountain hydrangea" only under "Other common names". NC State's dedicated page lists Blood-on-the-Snow, Mountain Hydrangea, Sawtooth Hydrangea and Tea of Heaven in an alphabetized Common Name(s) list that ranks nothing, so its first entry does not make that name primary. The assigned name Mountain Hydrangea appears in both sources but is led by neither. NC State lists the former names Hydrangea macrophylla acuminata and Hydrangea macrophylla var serrata, and RHS lists the synonym Hydrangea macrophylla subsp. serrata. NC State describes this as a smaller, more compact plant with smaller leaves and flowers. It is kept separate from the landed Hydrangea macrophylla, and no macrophylla content was borrowed.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Plant Type field) lists the values "Poisonous" and "Shrub"; the Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics field that follows it is a separate field (Deciduous). The page has no Poison block, so no poison-part list, symptom list or severity rating is stated, and "Poisonous" is not scoped to any animal. NC State's separate Problems field carries three tags: Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. RHS (Potentially harmful field) states: "Skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". RHS gives no symptoms and does not name which plant part is harmful. NC State's Edibility field says the leaves can be used to make a sweet tea and can be distilled to create a sweetener, and gives no preparation times or conditions. That sits uneasily with its own Poisonous tag and with RHS's "Harmful if eaten" for pets, so treat edibility as unresolved and do not feed any part to people or pets.
unknowns: MoBot's dedicated page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=292385) fails TLS verification for command-line fetchers but renders in a browser. It reads 'Common Name: hydrangea' (genus-level, not a lead-name candidate), 'Sun: Part shade', 'Water: Medium', 'Height: 2.00 to 4.00 feet' and 'Spread: 2.00 to 4.00 feet', and states 'Tolerates full sun only if grown with consistently moist soils.' and 'Leaves of Hydrangea serrata can be used to make a sweet tea, hence the sometimes used common name of tea of heaven for this shrub.' verify_quotes cannot check this host, so no MoBot citations were landed.

common_name: RHS leads with saw-toothed hydrangea and lists mountain hydrangea only as an 'other' name. NC State's alphabetized list ranks nothing. The assigned name Mountain Hydrangea is therefore not led by either dedicated page; saw-toothed hydrangea was chosen from RHS's subtitle. MoBot's dedicated page leads with the genus-level 'hydrangea', which is not a usable species common name, so RHS's saw-toothed hydrangea stands.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags and RHS's 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten'. NC State's Plant Type 'Poisonous' is not scoped to any animal. Neither source gives symptoms, poison parts or a severity rating, and NC State has no Poison block. RHS also warns of a skin allergen and says to wear gloves when handling.

is_edible=true is conditional and contested. NC State's Edibility field says the leaves can be used to make a sweet tea and can be distilled to create a sweetener, with no times or conditions. The same page tags the plant Poisonous, and RHS says it is harmful if eaten by pets. No preparation instructions are available, so this should not be shown as a food plant without a caveat.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun and Partial Shade, but its tags mark the plant '#full sun tolerant', its prose says it 'will grow best in light to open shade', and it warns 'In warmer climates, a location protected from hot sun will keep the foliage and flowers from prematurely fading or scorching'. RHS's Position field lists only Partial shade ('grow in sun if soil remains reliably moist' is conditional), and MoBot gives 'Sun: Part shade' and 'Tolerates full sun only if grown with consistently moist soils.' full_sun was dropped as a tolerance. No species-specific direct-sun hours were found, so direct_sun_hours_max is null.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral. The open-ended acid band gives no floor and RHS accepts alkaline soil, so both pH bounds are null. NC State says flower color varies from blue to pink relative to soil pH; this is not part of the schema and was not borrowed from macrophylla.

water_regime=keep_moist rests on NC State's 'In warmer climates, a location protected from hot sun will keep the foliage and flowers from prematurely fading or scorching and it will flower more prolifically with consistent summer watering.' Counterpoints, disclosed and not used as support: RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' and NC State's Soil Drainage values Good Drainage and Moist describe soil; MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' (mid-scale). No source gives a watering interval, dry-down target or check depth, so those fields are null.

Mature size is anchored on NC State's Dimensions block (Height 2-4 ft, Width 2-4 ft, i.e. 24-48 in). RHS gives a different Max Height and Max Spread of 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in), which is larger. RHS's own prose says 'not usually more than 1.2m high and often much smaller'.

No admissible source states a chill-damage onset temperature, day or night temperature range, humidity, light in foot-candles or fertilizer schedule. RHS's H4 rating and NC State's zones 6a-9b are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset figures. is_houseplant is false: no source addresses indoor culture, and NC State lists Landscape Location Container, Patio, Small Space and Woodland with USDA zones 6a-9b.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's page-title parenthetical lists Giant Arborvitae first, then Western Redcedar and Western Red-cedar. RHS's page title gives western red cedar, and RHS's Other common names list includes giant arbor-vitae. Western Red Cedar was chosen to match the RHS page title.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's 'Potentially harmful' field reads: 'Harmful if eaten; skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'. It names no animal, lists no poison part and gives no symptoms. NC State's page for this species has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags. The RHS handling warning is therefore not evidence of cat or dog toxicity.
unknowns: The Missouri Botanical Garden page for Thuja plicata (kempercode=b432, redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be loaded: TLS/connect errors in the sandbox, so none of its content was used. The UF/IFAS EDIS/Ask IFAS fact sheet ST630 returns HTTP 410 (no longer available). Only NC State and RHS were usable.
toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity evidence is RHS's 'Harmful if eaten; skin allergen' tag, which names no animal. NC State has no Poison block or cat/dog tags for this species.
is_edible is false only on the strength of RHS's 'Harmful if eaten' tag. No admissible source addresses food use. RHS gives no poison part or symptom list.

water_regime left null: NC State says it 'prefers consistently moist, well-drained soil' (a soil preference, not a watering instruction). RHS's moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'. Neither gives a watering instruction. NC State also says 'It does not tolerate drought or dry winds'.

soil_drainage set to moderate: NC State's drainage tags are Good Drainage plus Occasionally Wet (also a wet-soil-tolerant tag), and its prose says moist, well-drained. RHS says moist but well-drained. No source makes consistently wet soil a requirement, so moisture_retentive was not used.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) (open-ended) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral, so a ceiling from the Neutral band is not supportable.

RHS size fields are open-ended (Max Height 'Higher than 12 metres', Max Spread 'wider than 8 metres'). RHS prose says an ultimate height of up to 35m, which exceeds NC State's 50-70 ft range. NC State's Dimensions block was used as the anchor, so sizes are the NC State cultivated-landscape figures (50-70 ft = 600-840 in; 15-25 ft = 180-300 in).
NC State rates Growth Rate as 'Medium' in its structured field but its prose says 'the growth rate is fast, typically 2 to 3 feet per year'. There is no growth-rate field in this schema.
RHS lists full sun and partial shade, and NC State lists full sun, partial shade and dappled sunlight (mapped to part_shade). Both agree, so no value was dropped.

Not enough admissible-source support for temperature ranges, humidity, light in foot-candles, direct_sun_hours_max, fertilizing, watering intervals or pollinator attraction, so those are null. NC State's Wildlife Value text covers birds and mammals, not pollination.
The hybrid 'Green Giant' arborvitae (T. standishii x T. plicata) was not used as a source for size or growth. Thuja occidentalis and Juniperus virginiana are separate species and were not used.

records.name_note: Both loaded admissible pages dedicated to this taxon lead with Abyssinian: RHS renders 'Abyssinian gladiolus' as the common name under its Gladiolus murielae heading, and the first item of NC State's Common Name(s) list is Abyssinian (the list is alphabetical and ranks nothing). NC State's list also carries Fragrant Gladiolus, Peacock Gladiolus, Peacock Orchid and Sword Lily, and its description calls the plant 'fragrant gladiolus'. Despite the name Peacock Orchid, the plant is in the iris family (Iridaceae), not an orchid. NC State lists Acidanthera bicolor and Acidanthera murielae under 'Previously known as', and RHS lists both among its synonyms. The Missouri Botanical Garden page (kempercode a454) could not be loaded, so it was not used.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Tags line for Gladiolus murielae reads "#full sun tolerant #bulb #white flowers #maroon #summer bulbs #showy flowers #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #herbaceous perennial #corm #cutting garden #perennial #fragrant flowers", and its Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses. The NC State page carries no Poison block, no poison-part list and no symptom list, so no severity, plant part or symptoms are known from it. RHS's Potentially harmful note on the same species reads: "Ornamental bulbs; not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". The RHS pets statement names no animal, so only NC State's cat and dog tags and Problems values support toxic_to_pets. The sources address different parts: NC State's Flower Value To Gardener field lists Edible (with Fragrant, Good Cut and Showy), with no preparation or amount, while RHS says the ornamental bulbs are not to be eaten.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: neither admissible page frames the plant as a houseplant; NC State says to use it in the border of garden beds or containers and lists Landscape Location Container, Pond, Small Space and Walkways with USDA zones 7a-10b.

is_edible left null: NC State lists Edible under Flower Value To Gardener with no preparation or amount, and RHS says 'Ornamental bulbs; not to be eaten'. The two statements concern different parts (flowers, corms), and no source says the plant is grown or used for food, so no edibility is asserted. Nothing was borrowed from Gladiolus x hortulanus.
toxicity: NC State has only Problem-for-Cats/Dogs/Horses tags and no Poison block, poison part or symptoms; RHS's pets warning names no animal.
Missouri Botanical Garden page (kempercode a454) could not be loaded from this sandbox, so no MoBot evidence is used.
soil_ph_min/max left null: RHS says only 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' with no numeric range; NC State gives no pH field.

water_regime and the watering day fields left null: NC State's 'moist soil with good drainage' is a soil adjective and 'provide water during dry spells' is not a regime; RHS gives moisture as 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'.
soil_drainage set to moderate from NC State Good Drainage plus Occasionally Wet and RHS moist but well-drained; not set to fast.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's '6 or more hours' is the minimum for full sun and no species-specific maximum is stated. RHS lists south-, east- or west-facing aspect and sheltered exposure.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's dedicated page has the bare binomial as its H1. Its page-title parenthetical reads (King's Flower, Pineapple Lily), and its alphabetized Common Name(s) list is in the same order (King's Flower, then Pineapple Lily), so NC State's lead is King's Flower. RHS's dedicated page gives 'pineapple lily' as its common name beneath the H1 Eucomis comosa (page title 'Eucomis comosa | pineapple lily') and lists 'pineapple flower' under Other common names. Pineapple Lily is RHS's dedicated-page lead and is also on NC State's list, so it was chosen. Synonyms: NC State lists Asphodelus comosus and Eucomis punctata as 'Previously known as'; RHS lists Eucomis punctata under Synonyms.
records.cool_rest_note: NC State Bulb Storage field: store bulbs dry at 55-68 degrees F (13-20 degrees C) in Zone 6; hardy in Zones 7-8. This is a regional overwintering/storage instruction, not a damage-onset temperature.
unknowns: Toxicity: no admissible source found that names Eucomis comosa and addresses cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. The NC State page for this species has no Poison or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs block. Pet-safety pages from UGA, Penn State, Clemson and UF/IFAS surfaced in search results do not name this species and were not used, and nothing was borrowed from true lilies (Lilium).
Edibility: no admissible source addresses eating this plant, so is_edible is null. Nothing was borrowed from Ananas comosus or Acca sellowiana, which share the 'pineapple' name.

MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org / www.missouribotanicalgarden.org) taxonid=281878 could not be loaded here (connection error through the sandbox, then a certificate error). Nothing from MoBot is used, and its common-name, culture and size content is unchecked. Clemson HGIC returned HTTP 403, and no UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page for this species was found.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source describes indoor houseplant culture. NC State lists Landscape Location as Container and Patio and carries the tags #container plant and #patio; RHS's suggested planting locations are outdoor garden types (City and courtyard gardens, Coastal, Cottage and informal garden, Flower borders and beds, Wall side borders).

water_regime is null. NC State says it prefers a well-watered but well-drained organically rich soil and to keep the soil moist but not wet or soggy during flowering. That is a seasonal, flowering-period statement, and bulbs are stored dry in cold zones, so no single regime token was set. RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'.

soil_drainage moderate rests on RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained' and on NC State's Soil Drainage field 'Good Drainage', its Soil Texture values High Organic Matter and Loam (Silt), and its prose 'It prefers a well-watered but well-drained organically rich soil.' NC State's Soil Drainage field alone says only 'Good Drainage'.

soil_base garden_bed rests on RHS's species Suggested planting locations list, which includes 'Flower borders and beds', and on NC State's in-ground planting instructions ('Plant this bulb 8" (20 cm) deep, spacing bulbs 6-12 in. (15 cm) apart; one per 6-in. pot.'). NC State also says 'These bulbs grow well in containers, with the tips of the bulbs at the soil surface.' and lists Landscape Location as Container and Patio. RHS's Cultivation line is genus-level Eucomis text and is not used.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' and NC State gives no pH.

Size differs by source. NC State's own page gives 18-24 in height and 18-24 in width, and these were used. RHS gives Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), with stems to 75cm.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun and part_shade. NC State's structured Light field lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and NC State's prose says nothing about light. RHS's structured Position field lists 'Full sun' only; RHS is a UK source, not a North American structured field, and no source carries a species scorch warning, so part_shade is kept. MoBot, the other North American source, could not be loaded. RHS's Cultivation sentence 'Plant 15cm deep in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered position in full sun.' is genus-level Eucomis text, identical on RHS's Eucomis bicolor and Eucomis pole-evansii profiles, and is not used as species evidence. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the hour ranges in NC State's Light field are the site-wide light-category legend, not species prose.
chill_damage_f is null: NC State's Zones 7-8 hardy and Zone 6 storage figures and RHS's H4 rating are hardiness or storage guidance, not damage-onset temperatures.
No fertilizer, humidity, indoor light or day/night temperature guidance exists on the admissible pages read, so those fields are null.

records.name_note: The requested label was "European Fan Palm", but the two admissible dedicated pages I could load lead with different names. RHS's browser page title for this exact taxon is "Chamaerops humilis | dwarf fan palm", and its separate "Other common names" field lists "African hair palm, European fan palm". NC State's page-title parenthetical for this taxon reads "(Dwarf Palm, European Fan Palm, Mediterranean Fan Palm)"; its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and shows the same three names in the same order. NC State's Description prose refers to the plant as "The European fan palm". "European Fan Palm" therefore appears in both sources but leads neither page title or list. I chose RHS's lead "dwarf fan palm" (title-cased); NC State's lead "Dwarf Palm" is the alternative. MoBot and UF/IFAS could not be loaded, so they could not weigh in.
records.toxicity_detail: No pet-toxicity (cat or dog) statement was found on either admissible page that could be loaded for this species, so toxic_to_pets is null. NC State's Leaf Description says: "The petioles are armed with numerous sharp, needle-like spines." This is the page's description of the leaf stalks (to 3-4 ft long), not a stated handling instruction. NC State also lists "Spines" under its Appendage field.
unknowns: MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be loaded: the sandbox TLS check failed on that host, and the verifier skips it anyway. UF/IFAS FP123 (ask.ifas.ufl.edu) returns HTTP 410 Gone, and Clemson HGIC's page for this name returned 403. The only other admissible pages that turned up (HGIC palms, PSU palms as houseplants, UGA lists) cover several species, so none were used. All fields rest on the NC State and RHS pages for this exact taxon.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: neither NC State nor RHS carries a poison, Problem-for-Cats/Dogs or pet statement for Chamaerops humilis. Left null; do not borrow Cycas revoluta or Sabal minor.
is_edible and attracts_pollinators: neither page addresses eating or pollinators (no NC State Attracts field, no RHS pollinator tag), so both are null.

soil_drainage left null: NC State gives only 'Good Drainage' with no moisture field, and RHS gives only 'Well–drained'. A bare well-drained reading is ambiguous. NC State also says 'Overwatering can cause root rot and stem rot', and that once established the plant 'withstands drought and heat'.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's band is 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' while RHS gives 'Acid or Neutral', so the two do not agree on a floor or ceiling.

water_regime and the interval fields are left null. NC State gives no watering instruction beyond drought tolerance once established. RHS's care text is for growing under glass or as a houseplant: 'water moderately' when in growth, sparingly in winter. That fits no enum token, and "feed with a balanced fertiliser once a month" states a cadence in words, scoped only to "When in growth" with no named months and no strength, so no numeric interval, active months or strength is derived.
Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles and chill damage: no admissible loaded page states them. RHS hardiness H4 and NC State zones 8a-11b are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' and 'Partial Shade (...2-6 hours)' are the light-category definitions attached to the Light field, not species-specific prose.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade; its Description says it is 'easily grown in a bright sunny location (but tolerates partial shade)'. RHS lists Position 'Partial shade' (UK-calibrated). Values are full_sun and part_shade, mapping NC State's Partial Shade (2-6 hours direct sun) to part_shade.

soil_base standard_potting rests on RHS's houseplant/under-glass cultivation sentence (loam-based compost). NC State says only that it 'is not particular about soil type, as long as it is well-drained'.

Size: NC State's Dimensions give Height 6-15 ft (72-180 in) and Width 6-20 ft (72-240 in). RHS's UK figures are smaller: Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in) and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in), over a 20-50 year time to maturity. NC State was used as the anchor.
NC State's Plant Type field lists Houseplant, Perennial, Shrub and Tree. Its Cultivars section names var. cerifera and 'Volcano'; no cultivar sizes are used.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b116 (mixed gaps: a climbing rose, shrubs, a conifer, bulbs and a palm) landed from the post-audit records.
